title: The sage puts himself last
hookLine: heaven and earth last because they don't live for themselves; the sage puts himself last (Tao Te Ching 7)
carry: what doesn't live for itself lasts
tomorrow: the highest good is like water

cards: A four-way stop, late afternoon. Two cars arrive at the same moment. One driver waves: go ahead.
The other waves back: no, you. A little dance of hands through windshields, then somebody goes, and both drivers are smiling as they pull away. Nobody lost anything but a few seconds.
And for a moment, two strangers who'll never meet were on the same side. Chapter seven of the Tao Te Ching is about the strange strength of going last, and it starts with the sky and the ground.

teach.b: First, heaven and earth last. Legge's translation opens: "Heaven is long-enduring and earth continues long." Why?
Because, the chapter answers, they don't live for themselves. The sky doesn't hoard its rain; the ground doesn't keep its harvest. They give everything away, and they go on and on.

Second, the sage puts himself last. In Legge's words, "the sage puts his own person last, and yet it is found in the foremost place." He treats his own self as if it were outside him, and yet his self is kept safe.
Not grasping, and somehow not lost.

teach.h: NOT A TRICK FOR GETTING AHEAD.
teach.b: Third, not a trick for getting ahead. The chapter ends with a question: isn't it because the sage has no private aims that his aims are fulfilled? Readers take this two ways.

Some hear a strategy: hold back, and you'll end up ahead. Others say that going last in order to be first misses it, because the point was not to live for yourself at all. The chapter doesn't settle it.

At the end of a parable where workers hired at the last hour are paid first, the King James reads: "So the last shall be first, and the first last." The parable keeps its own meaning, and the chapter keeps its own.
What they share is an upside-down order.

how: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter seven into small daily choices, stepping back in lines, conversations and traffic, as a way of not living only for themselves.

finishing a race slower than everyone else

games.q: you and another driver reach a four-way stop at the same moment. you're the sage of chapter seven. what do you do?
o: go first: you were there a split second earlier.
sit still and wait for them to make a mistake.
games.why: the sage puts his own person last, and the chapter says that is somehow how he ends up in front.

practice: Picture the places today where there'll be a small line: a doorway, a coffee counter, a merge onto the highway, a turn to talk in a meeting.

See yourself stepping back at one of them with a small gesture, go ahead, and notice what it costs, which is probably very little. If you pray, you can offer that small step back; if not, just rehearse the gesture.

wordCard.voice: Last. In chapter seven, heaven and earth last because they don't live for themselves, and the sage who puts himself last is found in front. Today's word.
